July 31, 2026

VIA ETARIFF
Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Esq., Secretary
Carlos Clay, Deputy Secretary
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission 
888 First Street, N.E.
Washington, DC  20426
Re:	Duke Energy Florida, LLC, Surplus Interconnection Service Revisions to Attachment J to Joint OATT, Docket No. ER26-___-000
Dear Secretaries:
Pursuant to Section 205 of the Federal Power Act and Part 35 of the regulations of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”)), Duke Energy Florida, LLC (“DEF”) submits revisions to Attachment J (Large Generator Interconnection Procedures (“LGIP”) and the Large Generator Interconnection Agreement (“LGIA”)) under Tariff Volume No. 4, its Joint Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Joint OATT”) to include the surplus interconnection service reforms described below.  
DEF’s affiliates Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC (“DEC”) and Duke Energy Progress, LLC (“DEP”) are concurrently submitting a similar filing to revise their Attachment K (LGIP and LGIA) to the Joint OATT to include almost identical surplus interconnection service reforms.
Capitalized terms used but not defined herein have the meaning ascribed to them in the Joint OATT.  This transmittal letter contains information required by Part 35 of the regulations of the Commission.  In the event of any inconsistencies, discrepancies, or conflicts between the language in this transmittal letter and the terms of the Joint OATT, the Joint OATT shall control.
BACKGROUND TO SURPLUS INTERCONNECTION SERVICE
Order Nos. 845 and 845-A
The Commission issued Order No. 845 reforming the pro forma LGIP and pro forma LGIA to enhance the interconnection process, including requiring transmission providers to “create a process for interconnection customers to use surplus interconnection service at existing points of interconnection.”  The Commission mandated that such process must be one that “(1) includes a definition of surplus interconnection service consistent with the Final Rule; (2) provides an expedited interconnection process outside of the interconnection queue for surplus interconnection service, consistent with the Final Rule; (3) allows affiliates of the original interconnection customers to use surplus interconnection service for another interconnecting generating facility consistent with the Final Rule; (4) allows for the transfer of surplus interconnection service that the original interconnection customer or one of its affiliates does not intend to use; and (5) specifies what reliability-related studies and approvals are necessary to provide surplus interconnection service and to ensure the reliable use of surplus interconnection service.”  
The Commission declined to adopt pro forma surplus study agreements and interconnection agreements.  Instead, the Commission afforded transmission providers the discretion to develop their own surplus agreements to “give transmission providers flexibility to establish agreements appropriate for their region (e.g., they may be different for RTO/ISO and non-RTO/ISO regions) and the unique conditions of each agreement for surplus interconnection service” and submit them for filing to the Commission on an individual ad hoc basis or as pro forma agreements subject to the “consistent with or superior to” legal standard of review.
The Duke Southeast Utilities (comprised of DEF, DEC and DEP) submitted compliance filings in which they explained that they had posted their process on their OASIS sites.  The Duke Southeast Utilities submitted subsequent compliance filings in which they inserted a new section, Section 3.3.2 (Process for Surplus Interconnection Service Requests), in their LGIP which provided for and described an expedited process for interconnection customers to use surplus interconnection service.  The Commission issued an order partially accepting the compliance filings effective as of May 22, 2019 subject to a further compliance filing.  After the Duke Southeast Utilities submitted further compliance filings, the Commission issued a delegated letter order accepting all such Order No. 845 compliance filings.
Order Nos. 2023 and 2023-A
In Order Nos. 2023 and 2023-A, the Commission sought to further improve the surplus interconnection process.  Specifically, the Commission adopted language in the pro forma LGIP that requires “transmission providers to allow interconnections to access the surplus interconnection service process once the original interconnection customer has an executed LGIA or requests the filing of an unexecuted LGIA.”  The Commission found that the surplus interconnection service would benefit interconnection customers by allowing other generating facilities the opportunity to use the unused interconnection service earlier in the process, which will “increase the overall efficiency of the interconnection queue and in turn ensure just and reasonable rates.” The Commission clarified that the reform “does not modify how the surplus interconnection service process is conducted, but rather addresses when a request for surplus interconnection service may be submitted.”  The Commission also clarified that “the original interconnection customer must have an LGIA in place, either executed or requested to be filed unexecuted with the Commission, prior to the transmission provider tendering any LGIA for surplus interconnection service.”
DEF submitted Order Nos. 2023 and 2023-A compliance filings for Attachment J in Docket No. ER24-679.  The Commission issued a series of orders accepting such compliance filings effective as of April 1, 2024.  The Commission also accepted a clean-up filing to Attachment J to incorporate all accepted tariff record versions of Attachment J into one consolidated version.
HISTORY OF GENERATOR INTERCONNECTION REFORMS, CURRENT SURPLUS PROCESS, AND NEED FOR SURPLUS REFORMS
History of Generator Interconnection Reforms
The Duke Southeast Utilities have experienced rapid and sustained growth in their generator interconnection queues in the past and are currently experiencing unprecedented load growth in their regions.  To address these issues, the utilities have systematically been pursuing reforms of their FERC-jurisdictional interconnection processes over the last several years in order to accelerate the ability for new generation to interconnect and serve the growing load.  DEC and DEP were early adopters of cluster processes and DEF was the first utility to receive regulatory approval of its Order No. 2023 cluster process.  The Duke Southeast Utilities also received approval of generator replacement reforms to allow current generation to be replaced with new generation more expeditiously and outside the traditional generator interconnection cluster process framework.
As it pertains to this filing, the Duke Southeast Utilities have pursued regulatory approval of pro forma versions of various generator interconnection-related agreements in an effort to streamline the interconnection process.  The Commission has approved each of those pro forma agreements and a summary of the history of these regulatory reforms is set forth below. 
Pro Forma Provisional Interconnection Study Agreement.  The Commission approved a pro forma Provisional Interconnection Study Agreement for DEC and DEP in Docket No. ER24-2431-002 in March 2025 and for DEF in Docket No. ER26-705-000 in February 2026.
Pro Forma Provisional LGIA.  The Commission approved a pro forma Provisional Interconnection Study Agreement for DEC and DEP in Docket No. ER24-2431-002 in March 2025 and for DEF in Docket No. ER26-705-000 in February 2026.
Pro Forma Engineering and Procurement Agreement.  The Commission approve a pro forma Engineering and Procurement Agreement for DEC and DEP in Docket No. ER26-1399-000 in April 2026, and for DEF in Docket No. ER26-1398-000 in April 2026.
These regulatory reforms have produced tremendous benefits on a collective basis, allowing interconnection requests to be studied on a first-ready clustered basis, new generation to more expeditiously replace existing generation while utilizing existing transmission infrastructure, new generation to interconnect on a provisional basis while awaiting completion of network upgrades needed for full interconnection service, and long lead-time equipment to be procured under engineering and procurement agreements to expedite interconnections requiring such equipment.
Current Surplus Process
As stated above, the Duke Southeast Utilities’ current process for surplus service is contained in their LGIPs at Section 3.3.2 (Process for Surplus Interconnection Service Requests) and is not being changed in this filing.  However, the Duke Southeast Utilities have taken the opportunity to include more implementation details in their Surplus Generator Interconnection Procedure posted on their OASIS sites (the “Procedure”) to provide more transparency and information about how the utilities perform studies to evaluate surplus interconnection service requests.  
The testimony of Mr. Orvane Piper included with this filing provides an explanation of the current study process that the Duke Southeast Utilities utilize in evaluating such requests.  He describes that the Duke Southeast Utilities have revised their OASIS posting describing the current Procedure in an effort to provide more transparency and awareness to customers as to how the utilities will conduct studies to evaluate potential impacts of surplus interconnection service requests.  Mr. Piper discusses that the Duke Southeast Utilities have revised their Procedure in the following ways.  First, the Procedure has been revised to note the conditions under which surplus interconnection service requests will be studied for energy storage devices to be located at existing solar sites.  Second, the Procedure has been revised to identify the base cases to be used in the studies.  Third, the Procedure has been revised to identify the study methodology to be used in performing the studies, which will include (1) power flow analysis, (2) reactive capability analysis, (3) short circuit analysis, and (4) stability analysis.  Finally, the Procedure has been revised to discuss whether such studies consider impacts to affected systems and how studies will be performed for hybrid facilities.  With respect to hybrid facilities and studies for storage components of those facilities, he states that the Duke Southeast Utilities conduct studies of the storage components of hybrid facilities according to their storage practice methodologies posted on their OASIS sites.
Need for Surplus Reforms
The testimony of Gary Sullivan included with this filing provides an explanation of the load growth that DEF is experiencing in its region, need for additional generation to serve such growing load, and the efficiencies that would be created by the proposed reforms to facilitate surplus interconnection service to bring on generation in the most efficient manner in light of the need to expedite reliable generator interconnections and accommodating unprecedented load growth.
First of all, DEF is experiencing continuing load growth in its region which will drive the need for generation, some of which could be served by surplus generation that takes advantage of surplus interconnection service existing at points of interconnection on the DEF system.  In its 2026 Ten-Year Site Plan filed with the Florida Public Service Commission (“FPSC”) in April 2026, DEF described its continuing load growth measured by annual sales growth across all retail customer classes comprised of residential, commercial and industrial.  Mr. Sullivan highlights in his testimony that as an example of its continuing load growth, DEF experienced that “an expanding customer added 1 GWH to the system in 2025 and is projected to grow to 52 GWH by 2029” which is a substantial increase in expected load from just one customer.
Secondly, DEF anticipates that it may be requested to provide service to large load customers that seek to locate in DEF’s region.  The FPSC underscored the possible impact that large load customers pose in Florida in its Review of the 2025 Ten Year Site Plans of Florida’s Electric Utilities, emphasizing that “Florida’s electric industry is experiencing heightened demand for power from customers influenced by the potential expansion of data centers.” The FPSC explained that “Florida utilities recognize the associated substantial increase in load to serve such customers and, to the extent such load materialize, they will require significant new infrastructure in both generation and transmission.”  The FPSC noted that “[i]ncreased loads can be met on the utility side by improving existing generation and transmission infrastructure to allow more energy-efficient production and delivery of electricity or with the addition of new resources such as battery energy storage.” In anticipation of requests to serve large load customers, DEF proactively filed a Large Load Customer Rate Schedule with the FPSC in September 2025 to pursue regulatory reforms related to certain large load customers.  Large load customers will drive the need for generation to serve them, and new generators that utilize surplus interconnection service could potentially assist in serving new load customers.
Third, the Duke Southeast Utilities have witnessed a substantial increase in Interconnection Customers that are interested in surplus interconnection service.  Specifically, there have been 14 requests for surplus interconnection service in the regions, representing 759.2 MW/3,036.8 MWh of generation seeking to interconnect to the grid on a surplus basis.  In the last 2.5 years, the requests have represented 3 times the number of requests received in the first 5 years the service was available.  These requests represent a significant amount of new generation that may be able to interconnect more expeditiously and utilize the extra, or surplus, interconnection service. 
Fourth, the Duke Southeast Utilities anticipate that interconnection customers seeking to interconnect an electric storage resource at an existing solar generation facility site may wish to take advantage of surplus interconnection service at those sites to do so.  Mr. Sullivan explains in his testimony that the installation of an energy storage device that utilizes surplus interconnection service at an existing solar site provides a ready site for the storage device and allows the interconnection capability of the site to be used more effectively without increasing the maximum output at the point of interconnection at the site.  The practical value of surplus interconnection service is that the storage device can assist in turning an existing variable solar site into a more dispatchable resource, while respecting the existing interconnection limits and parameters.  Additionally, the storage device can provide firm winter and summer capacity to the existing solar sites, turning a low-capacity solar resource to a more firm capacity solar-plus-storage resource.  Mr. Sullivan provides data in his testimony that there are 23 operational solar sites in the Duke Southeast Utilities’ regions, collectively, that could have surplus interconnection service requests submitted to install a surplus generator at those sites, representing 1,691 MW of potential surplus generation.  He also states that there are 28 solar sites not yet in operation (either in the interconnection agreement phase or construction phrase) in those regions that could have surplus interconnection service requests submitted to install a surplus generator at those sites, representing 2,272 MW of potential surplus generation.

In sum, unprecedented load growth and the need to bring on new generation to serve it cause a need to pursue surplus reforms to the interconnection process which will create efficiencies for surplus interconnection service and reduce regulatory timelines for administering conforming surplus interconnection service-related agreements.
APPLICABLE COMMISSION PRECEDENT
There is ample Commission precedent supporting the adoption by various transmission providers of pro forma surplus study agreements, as well as tariff revisions to effectuate improvements to the surplus interconnection service process.  There is also a long history of FERC approval of Surplus LGIAs and Energy Displacement Agreements filed on an individual basis as discussed below.  DEF posits that its proposed adoption of pro forma versions of each of these agreements meets the “consistent with or superior to” legal standard as discussed in Section V of this letter because (a) they enhance the interconnection process, which was a stated goal of the Commission in Order No. 845 and (b) they speed up the interconnection process, which was a stated goal of the Commission in Order No. 2023.        
Pro Forma Surplus Study Agreements
With respect to the pro forma Surplus Interconnection Service Study Agreement, six transmission providers have sought and obtained Commission approval of pro forma surplus interconnection study agreements.
Florida Power & Light Company: The Commission approved a pro forma Surplus Interconnection Study Agreement as Appendix 5 to its LGIP.
Nevada Power Company: The Commission approved a pro forma Surplus Interconnection Service System Impact Study Agreement as Appendix 2A to its LGIP and a pro forma Surplus Interconnection Service Facilities Study Agreement as Appendix 3A to its LGIP.
NorthWestern Corporation: The Commission approved a pro forma Surplus Interconnection Study Agreement as Appendix 5A to its LGIP.
Tri-State Generation and Transmission Association, Inc.:  The Commission approved a pro forma Surplus Interconnection Service Impact Study Agreement as Appendix 2A to its LGIP.
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.: The Commission approved a pro forma Surplus Interconnection Study Agreement as Attachment RR to its Interconnection Procedures.
Southwest Power Pool, Inc.: The Commission approved a pro forma Surplus Interconnection Service Impact Study Agreement and as Attachment 15 to its GIP and a pro forma Surplus Interconnection Service Facilities Study Agreement as Attachment 16 to its GIP.

 Individual Surplus LGIAs and Energy Displacement Agreements
With respect to the pro forma Surplus LGIA, the Duke Southeast Utilities modeled their pro forma versions of the agreement on their pro forma LGIAs, but also on the revisions to the LGIA revisions for surplus interconnection service filed by Xcel Energy Services Inc. on behalf of Public Service Company of Colorado (“PSCo”) on August 27, 2021 in Docket No. ER21-2781-000.  Transmission Provider also modeled its pro forma version of its Energy Displacement Agreement on the same agreement filed by PSCO in such docket.  The Commission accepted the PSCO agreements for filing via delegated letter order issued on October 11, 2021 in that same docket.

In turn, PSCo had modeled its agreements on similar agreements filed by the Midwest Independent Transmission System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”) on September 26, 2012 in Docket No. ER12-309-000.  The Commission accepted the MISO agreements for filing by letter order dated January 1, 2012.

Since that time, PacifiCorp has also modeled its individual Surplus LGIAs and Energy Displacement Agreements on the same PSCo agreements cited above.

There is now a well-established line of cases in which the Commission has approved individual Surplus LGIAs and Energy Displacement Agreements all modeled on the MISO and then PSCO agreements as described above. DESCRIPTION OF SURPLUS INTERCONNECTION SERVICE REVISIONS TO ATTACHMENT J
Overview
DEF is proposing tariff revisions to its LGIP to include the following changes: (a) changes to the Table of Contents in the LGIP to include the new pro forma surplus interconnection service related agreements as appendices thereto, (b) changes to LGIP Appendix 1 (Interconnection Request for a Large Generating Facility) to add an option for customers to identify that the Interconnection Request is for surplus service, (c) a pro forma Surplus Interconnection Service Study Agreement is proposed to be added as Appendix 18 to the LGIP, (d) a pro forma Surplus Interconnection Service Facilities Study Agreement is proposed to be added as Appendix 19 to the LGIP, (e) a pro forma Surplus Large Generator Interconnection Agreement (SLGIA) is proposed to be added as Appendix 20 to the LGIP, and (f) a pro forma Energy Displacement Agreement is proposed to be added as Appendix 21 to the LGIP.
LGIP Appendix 1 – Interconnection Request for a Large Generating Facility
LGIP Appendix 1 (Interconnection Request for a Large Generating Facility) has been revised to include an option to select Surplus Interconnection Service.  The language in red below is the same language as the Commission has approved in the DEC/DEP LGIP Appendix 1 in Attachment K to the Joint OATT.

	A proposed new Large Generating Facility.
	An increase in the generating capacity or a Material Modification of an existing Generating Facility.
	Replacement of Existing Generating Facility with no increase in capacity.

Pro Forma Surplus Interconnection Service Study Agreement
The terms of the pro forma Surplus Interconnection Study Agreement are based on the Commission’s pro forma Optional Interconnection Study Agreement. ER25-944 and ER25-945.

Recitals: Replace language that Interconnection Customer is “proposing to develop” a Large Generating Facility with “is proposing to utilize the Point of Interconnection under an existing Large Generator Interconnection Agreement” in recognition of the fact that there is already an executed LGIA for the Point of Interconnection;

Pro Forma Surplus LGIA
The pro forma Surplus LGIA is based on the Transmission Provider’s pro forma LGIA with the following modifications that provide terms and conditions for Surplus Interconnection Service.  All of these modifications have previously been approved by the Commission in the dockets identified below.

References to SLGIA:  replace all applicable occurrences of term “Standard Large Generator Interconnection Agreement” with “Surplus Large Generator Interconnection Agreement”; replace all applicable occurrences of term “LGIA” with “SLGIA.”  These revisions have previously been approved by the Commission in the Surplus LGIAs for DEC, DEP, PSCO and PacifiCorp in the dockets listed in Section III.C. above.
Article 1 (Definitions): 
New definition of “Energy Displacement Agreement” was added which reads as follows: “Energy Displacement Agreement shall mean an agreement between an Interconnection Customer with an Existing Generating Facility on the Transmission Provider’s Transmission System and an Interconnection Customer with a proposed Generating Facility seeking to interconnect with Surplus Interconnection Service. The Energy Displacement Agreement specifies the term of operation, the Generating Facility Interconnection Service limit, and the mode of operation for energy production (common or singular operation).”  This new definition has previously been approved by the Commission in the Surplus LGIAs for PSCO in the dockets listed in Section III.C. above.  
New definition of “Existing Generating Facility Interconnection Customer” was added which reads as follows:  “Existing Generating Facility Interconnection Customer shall mean any entity, including the Transmission Provider, Transmission Owner or any of the Affiliates or subsidiaries of either, with an LGIA for a Generating Facility that is either under construction or is in service, and has an unsuspended Interconnection Agreement with Transmission Provider.”  This new definition has previously been approved by the Commission in the Surplus LGIAs for PSCO in the dockets listed in Section III.C. above.
New definition of “SLGIA Milestones” was added which reads as follows: “SLGIA Milestone(s) shall mean milestones provided in Appendix B of this SLGIA.”  This new definition has previously been approved by the Commission in the Surplus LGIAs for PSCO and PacifiCorp in the dockets listed in Section III.C. above.  
New definition of “Surplus Large Generator Interconnection Agreement” was added which reads as follows: “Surplus Large Generator Interconnection Agreement (SLGIA) shall mean the interconnection agreement applicable to a Surplus Interconnection Request pertaining to a Large Generating Facility that is provided for in the Transmission Provider's Tariff.”  This new definition has previously been approved by the Commission in the Surplus LGIAs for PSCO and PacifiCorp in the dockets listed in Section III.C. above.

Pro Forma Energy Displacement Agreement
The Energy Displacement Agreement provides terms and conditions governing the net injection at the point of interconnection for the Generating Facility and the Existing Generating Facility, as well as the generation dispatch arrangements for the Generating Facility.  The Energy Displacement Agreement is an attachment to the Surplus LGIA.  A detailed discussion of the sections of the Displacement Agreement is set forth below.  The proposed pro forma Energy Displacement Agreement is substantially the same as has been approved by the Commission for MISO, PSCO, DEC, DEP and PacifiCorp in the dockets listed in Section III.C. above.
Section 1 discusses use of capitalized terms.  Section 2 sets forth terms for the net injection at the point of interconnection.  Section 3 discusses the generation dispatch arrangements for the Generating Facility which are set forth in an attachment to the agreement.  Section 4 states that the agreement shall be an attachment to the Surplus LGIA.  Section 5 sets forth the term of the agreement and Section 6 sets forth terms for termination of the agreement.  Sections 7 through 18 contain boilerplate contract provisions including breach, notice of breach, default, rights in the event of default, notices, governing law, waiver, amendment, severability, binding effect, no third party beneficiaries, no partnership, and multiple counterparts.
THE REFORMS MEET THE “CONSISTENT WITH OR SUPERIOR TO” STANDARD
The Commission established the pro forma LGIP and LGIA in Order No. 2003.  In adopting Order No. 2003, the Commission advised transmission providers that it will accept non-independent transmission provider variations from the pro forma LGIP and LGIA so long as the transmission provider can demonstrate that the variations are “consistent with or superior to” its final rules in Order No. 2003.  In Order No. 845, the Commission afforded transmission providers the discretion to develop their own surplus agreements and submit them for filing to the Commission on an individual ad hoc basis or as pro forma agreements subject to the “consistent with or superior to” legal standard of review.
Enhancing the Interconnection Process
One of the Commission’s stated goals in Order No. 845 was enhancing the interconnection process.  The inclusion of pro forma surplus interconnection service-related agreements in the Duke Southeast Utilities’ LGIPs will enhance interconnection service in five ways.
First, the use of pro forma agreements will achieve consistency and predictability with respect to the terms and conditions included in all of the agreements tendered to Interconnection Customers in the Duke Southeast Utilities’ regions.  The Commission has encouraged the use of pro forma agreements for this reason, stating that “[t]he availability of a pro forma FSA for the implementation of that funding option will help promote administrative efficiency and predictability.”
Second, the use of pro forma agreements will aid in contractual certainty of the terms and conditions to be included in each agreement since they will all be based on the pro forma versions.  Counterparties will be able to expect those certain terms and conditions to be included in the agreements tendered to them for execution, and thereby have increased contractual certainty of the provisions in those agreements.
Third, the use of pro forma agreements will improve Interconnection Customers’ awareness of the terms and conditions for surplus service that they can expect will be contained in the agreements since the agreements tendered to them will be based on the pro forma versions contained in the LGIPs.  
Fourth, the use of pro forma agreements will result in application of this language in a fair and non-discriminatory manner to all Interconnection Customers that request such service, again because the agreements tendered to them will be based on the pro forma versions.  The Commission has recognized that standardized agreements in tariffs reduce undue discrimination, ruling that “[a] standard set of procedures as part of the OATT for all jurisdictional transmission facilities will minimize opportunities for undue discrimination.”
Fifth, the use of pro forma agreements will eliminate risk of regulatory delays in approval of agreements or the issuance of regulatory orders rejecting the agreements.  Instead, the parties can be assured that entry into conforming surplus agreements will not require filing with the Commission or approval on a case-by-case basis.  The Commission has advised that even if transmission providers have interconnection policies and procedures in their tariffs, the Commission generally disfavors individual filings, stating in Order No. 2003 that “it has become apparent that the case-by-case approach is an inadequate and inefficient means to address interconnection issues.”
In sum, use of pro forma agreements will enhance consistency of their terms and conditions, contractual certainty concerning provisions in the agreements, Interconnection Customers’ awareness of the terms and conditions, application of terms and conditions in a fair and non-discriminatory manner for all customers, and reduce regulatory risks with filing agreements for Commission approval.  All of these outcomes resulting from the surplus reforms have the effect of enhancing the interconnection process for interconnection customers and for growing load that needs additional generation in the marketplace to serve it.
Speeding Up the Interconnection Process

One of the Commission’s stated goals in Order No. 2023 was speeding up the interconnection process.  The Commission has previously ruled that standard tariff procedures will “expedite the development of new generation.”  The Duke Southeast Utilities believe that its standardized tariff agreements (the pro formas submitted herein) will indeed speed up the interconnection process and expedite the development of new generation.  The explanation below describes how such reforms will have these intended effects.
First, the surplus study can begin as soon as the parties have executed a Surplus Interconnection Service Study Agreement that conforms to the pro forma version of the agreement.  Without a pro forma version, all the study agreements are considered non-conforming and are required to be filed with the Commission.  Work in furtherance of the study cannot begin until receipt of Commission order approving the study agreement.  In the future in which parties enter into a conforming study agreement, the Transmission Provider would be able to avoid a 61-day delay of the study while awaiting regulatory approval of the filed agreement and be able to begin the study right away.  The Transmission Provider is afforded 60 Business Days to complete the study according to LGIP Section 3.3.2(F), so avoiding a 61-day period for regulatory approval on a case-by-case basis reduces the amount of time to administer the study by almost half.  
Second, the parties will be able to negotiate the Surplus LGIA in less than the 60-day period provided by LGIP Section 3.3.2(J) because such negotiations will not start from scratch under one-off, individually drafted agreements but will be based on the Commission-approved pro forma version of the Surplus LGIA.  The pro forma version will be the template from which all Surplus LGIAs are drafted and it is expected that very few Surplus LGIAs will be non-conforming, barring exigent circumstances requiring unique customizations that would render them non-conforming.  The benefit of having terms and conditions for a Surplus LGIA that have already been approved by the Commission in a pro forma Surplus LGIA should allow the parties to significantly reduce the 60-day period for negotiations down to very few days if any.  The Commission has recognized this benefit provided by pro forma agreements, stating that “transmission owners and interconnection customers will no longer be required to negotiate the terms and conditions of each FSA.”
Third, the parties will be able to move forward quickly in effectuating their obligations under conforming Surplus LGIAs and Energy Displacement Agreements without having to wait to obtain regulatory approval of those agreements as long as such agreements conform to the pro forma versions.  Again, the 61-day period for regulatory approval will be eliminated and allow the parties to move forward in implementing these agreements.
Fourth, the transmission provider would normally be required to file a Notice of Cancellation of the Surplus Interconnection Service Study Agreement and the Surplus Interconnection Service Facilities Study Agreement once the studies have been completed and the reports have been provided to the customer and posted to OASIS.  The Duke Southeast Utilities have made a number of such filings in the past.  In the future, if the study agreements are conforming and not required to be filed with the Commission, then no Notice of Cancellation is required to be filed as well and saves another 61-day period for regulatory approval of the cancellation of each study agreement (so a combined 122-day period).  
In sum, the administration timelines within the surplus process should be reduced by about 304 days (61+60+61+61+61) by utilizing pro forma agreements (the Surplus Interconnection Service Study Agreement, Surplus Interconnection Service Facilities Study  Agreement, Surplus LGIA, and Energy Displacement Agreement) which currently are non-existent in the Joint OATT.  This speeds up the surplus process by almost 10 months, which is a significant amount of time and significant benefit to parties that wish to bring surplus generators online in an efficient manner. 
For all of these reasons set forth in subparts A and B of this section above, DEF has adequately demonstrated that the proposed surplus reforms are “consistent with” the Commission’s goals in Order No. 845 of enhancing interconnection and in Order No. 2023 of speeding up interconnection, provide the three benefits of surplus service identified in Order No. 845 as discussed above, and are “superior to” the currently existing Joint OATT which lacks these reforms which provide the significant benefits to interconnection customers and growing load as described above.
STAKEHOLDER ENGAGEMENT
On July 16, 2026, the Duke Southeast Utilities held two broad stakeholder meetings (one for DEF and one for DEC/DEP) to discuss its proposed reforms.  The meetings were held via Microsoft Teams Webinars and meeting invitations were sent to approximately 456 external parties including all transmission and generator interconnection customers of DEC, DEP and DEF.  Collectively, approximately 35 individuals attended the meeting, representing 27 different organizations comprised of existing generation owners, renewable energy developers, wholesale customers, trade industry organizations, and state consumer advocate organizations.  Sufficient time was set aside for questions from stakeholders in the meeting.  Materials for the stakeholder meeting, including the presentation to stakeholders, have been posted to each of the Duke Southeast Utilities’ OASIS websites.
CONTENTS OF FILING
The following documents are included in this filing in addition to the relevant tariff records:
This transmittal letter;
Clean copy of Attachment J;
Marked copy of Attachment J (against currently effective); 
Marked copy of pro forma Surplus Interconnection Service Study Agreement (against currently effective Optional Interconnection Study Agreement);
Marked copy of pro forma Surplus Interconnection Service Facilities Study Agreement (against currently effective Optional Interconnection Study Agreement);
Marked copy of pro forma Surplus LGIA (against currently effective LGIA); 
Testimony of Gary Sullivan; and
Testimony of Orvane Piper.
REQUESTED EFFECTIVE DATE
DEF requests that the Commission accept the revisions to Attachment J to the Joint OATT effective as of October 1, 2026.  No waiver is necessary to permit the requested effective date since such date is more than 61 days after the filing date of this tariff change.
INFORMATION REQUIRED BY 18 C.F.R. §35.13
The revisions to Attachment J do not change any rates that generator Interconnection Customers will be charged under the LGIP and LGIA.  Therefore, this filing is not a “rate change” within the meaning of section 35.13(a) of the Commission’s regulations and likewise is not a “rate increase” within the meaning of section 35.13(a)(2)(iii) of the Commission’s regulations. DEF is submitting this filing pursuant to the abbreviated procedures set forth in that section and requests any waivers necessary to permit it to do so.
Finally, the information required by 18 C.F.R. §§35.13(b) and (c) is as follows: the agreement of the customer has been obtained, and no expenses or costs in connection with these tariff revisions have been alleged or judged in any administrative or judicial proceeding to be illegal, duplicative, or unnecessary costs that are demonstrably the product of discriminatory employment practices.
COMMUNICATIONS
All correspondence should be addressed to the persons listed below.
SERVICE OF FILING
Per 18 C.F.R. § 385.2010(f)(2) which requires electronic service of FERC filings, this filing will be served by email on (a) the state regulatory commission having jurisdiction over DEF and (b) all transmission customers taking service from DEF under the Joint OATT.
CONCLUSION
For the reasons above, DEF requests that the Commission issue an order accepting the revisions to Attachment J to the Joint OATT for filing and grant the requested effective date.  Please contact the undersigned if you have any questions.
Respectfully submitted,
/s/ Ann L. Warren
Ann L. Warren
Associate General Counsel
Duke Energy Corporation
